lesson.title: One Data Point Shouldn't Be Able to Predict Its Neighbor
lesson.summary: The independence condition requires that observations, and their residuals, don't systematically influence or predict one another, a condition justified by study design (random sampling or random assignment) rather than by a plot.
lesson.body:
Independence means that individual observations, and by extension their residuals, don't systematically influence, predict, or move together with each other. This condition matters because the SE(b1) formula from two chapters back implicitly assumes every data point is contributing a fresh, unrelated piece of information. When observations are related to each other, clustered, repeated measurements on the same subject, or points that drift together over time, the data actually contain less independent information than the raw count n suggests, and standard errors computed as if n were the true amount of independent information come out too small. That makes t-statistics too large and p-values misleadingly tiny.

Unlike the other three conditions, independence usually cannot be checked by looking at a plot after the fact. It has to be reasoned about from how the data were collected. In an experiment, random assignment to treatment groups is what breaks any systematic connection between one unit's outcome and another's. In an observational study, random sampling from the population plays the same role: each individual is selected independently of every other, so there's no built-in mechanism linking their outcomes.

A classic violation is time series data. Suppose a city's daily temperature and ice cream sales are recorded for 60 consecutive days. Today's temperature is strongly related to yesterday's, heat waves and cold snaps both last several days, so the residuals from a regression of sales on temperature tend to run in streaks: several positive residuals in a row during an unusually warm stretch, several negative ones in a row during a cool one. That streaking pattern, sometimes visible when residuals are plotted against time rather than against x, is a sign of autocorrelation, a specific and common way independence fails.

Applied to the running example: if the six students were selected from a larger class and studied and took the quiz independently, no group study sessions where scores would rise or fall together, no copying, independence is a reasonable assumption. But if those six numbers were actually the same one student's scores on six different quizzes across a semester, independence would be shaky: performance on quiz 3 is plausibly related to performance on quiz 2 through the student's developing skill, fatigue, or motivation, violating the idea that each data point is a fresh, unrelated observation.

On the AP exam and in practice, independence is typically justified in writing rather than shown in a picture: point to random sampling or random assignment in the study's design, and, when sampling without replacement from a finite population, confirm the sample is less than about 10% of that population.
